Issues.Title: DBSC session authentication does not preserve the source scheme's per-request forwarding
Issues.Body:
## Summary

DBSC is registered over an existing cookie scheme, but once a session cookie exists, later authentication does not go back through the source scheme's per-request forwarding. When the source scheme's authenticate target can vary by request, for example through `ForwardDefaultSelector`, DBSC can establish a request user from a different target or partition than the one the source scheme would select for that request.

Related to #66478 (DBSC tracking), #68117 (API proposal), and the derived-scheme inheritance issues #69618 and #69619. The implementation was removed from .NET 11 by #69462 and backported by #69479, so this issue tracks a requirement for any future DBSC reintroduction rather than a .NET 11 servicing change.

## What is wrong

* Registration calls `AuthenticateAsync(RegistrationSourceScheme)`. That call honors the source scheme's forwarding for the registration request, and DBSC mints refresh and session cookies from the resulting principal without recording which effective target produced it.
* The generated DBSC policy scheme selects the session scheme based only on session-cookie presence. It does not re-evaluate the source scheme's `ForwardAuthenticate`, `ForwardDefaultSelector`, or `ForwardDefault` for the current request.
* Refresh authenticates the refresh scheme and mints a new session cookie without checking the source scheme's current-request target.
* `PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionAuthenticationOptions` redirects the application's default authenticate scheme to the DBSC policy scheme, so this substitution becomes the default authentication path.
* DBSC accepts this composition without an error, and the API surface does not document that source schemes with request-dependent forwarding are unsupported.

## Why it matters

* The invariant is that DBSC-derived authentication must resolve to the same effective source target as the wrapped scheme for the current request, or the unsupported composition must be rejected.
* Applications that partition cookie authentication per request, for example by selecting a partition-specific cookie scheme by host or path, cannot currently infer or enforce that requirement.

## Affected code

Permalinks point to `b3d5795c6f`, the last `main` commit before the DBSC removal.

* [`DeviceBoundSessionExtensions.cs:98-116`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/DeviceBoundSessionExtensions.cs#L98-L116) - policy-scheme selector chooses the session scheme based only on cookie presence.
* [`DeviceBoundSessionHandler.cs:87-172`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/DeviceBoundSessionHandler.cs#L87-L172) - registration authenticates the source scheme through its forwarding, then mints derived cookies without binding the effective target.
* [`DeviceBoundSessionHandler.cs:174-276`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/DeviceBoundSessionHandler.cs#L174-L276) - refresh mints session cookies without checking the source scheme's current-request target.
* [`PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionAuthenticationOptions.cs:25-39`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionAuthenticationOptions.cs#L25-L39) - default authenticate scheme redirected to the DBSC policy scheme.
* [`AuthenticationHandler.cs:204-221`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/Core/src/AuthenticationHandler.cs#L204-L221) - forwarding resolution (`ForwardAuthenticate`, then `ForwardDefaultSelector`, then `ForwardDefault`) that DBSC's later-authentication path does not reproduce.
* `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.DeviceBoundSessions` `0.11.0-rc.1.26425.128` - experimental prerelease package containing the implementation.

## Recommended fix

Selected approach: reject DBSC over source schemes whose authenticate target can vary by request.

* Add a source-scheme inspector that resolves the source scheme's forwarding configuration. Treat it as variable when `ForwardAuthenticate` is unset and `ForwardDefaultSelector` is set. Follow static `ForwardAuthenticate` and `ForwardDefault` chains, and handle policy-scheme sources.
* Prefer failing at startup through options validation with a clear message. Also enforce the check at runtime so an unsupported composition cannot mint or use derived cookies:
  * Registration: do not authenticate the source scheme or mint refresh and session cookies.
  * Policy scheme: do not select the session scheme; use the source scheme.
  * Refresh: do not mint a session cookie.
* Document supported source-scheme compositions on `AddDeviceBoundSession`.

A draft of the registration guard:

```csharp
if (Options.RegistrationSourceScheme is { } sourceScheme &&
    _sourceSchemeInspector.AuthenticateTargetCanVaryByForwarding(sourceScheme))
{
    Logger.RegistrationUnsupportedSourceScheme(sourceScheme);
    Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError;
    return;
}
```

Alternatives considered:

* Bind the resolved effective source target into protected refresh and session state at registration, then require the current request's source resolution to match it before the session scheme establishes a user and before refresh mints a session cookie. This supports the composition but adds per-request forwarding evaluation to the session path and more state to carry. It is a reasonable follow-up if forwarded sources should be supported.
* Document the limitation without enforcement. Rejected because callers cannot reliably detect whether a source scheme's target varies at runtime, and DBSC owns the substituted authentication decision.

Compatibility: no public API change is expected beyond documentation and possibly a validation error. Applications that currently compose DBSC over a request-dependent forwarding source will fail validation or stop receiving DBSC session authentication. Because the package is experimental and removed from .NET 11, apply this before any future DBSC package is published.

## Acceptance criteria

* [ ] A source scheme whose authenticate target can vary by request is rejected with a clear error, or DBSC enforces that the current request's effective source target matches the target bound at registration.
* [ ] For an unsupported composition, registration mints no refresh or session cookies, the policy scheme does not select the session scheme, and refresh mints no session cookie.
* [ ] Sources without forwarding, and sources with a static forwarding chain, behave as they do today.
* [ ] Tests use the real `AddCookie` and `AddDeviceBoundSession` registration path with a source scheme that uses `ForwardDefaultSelector` over two cookie schemes. They verify that a DBSC session established under one target does not authenticate a request that the source scheme resolves to the other target.
* [ ] `AddDeviceBoundSession` documentation lists the supported source-scheme compositions.
* [ ] #66478 records this requirement before DBSC is reintroduced.

Issues.Title: DBSC derived cookie schemes should inherit the source scheme's DataProtectionProvider
Issues.Body:
## Summary

The experimental DBSC implementation generates refresh and session cookie schemes from a source cookie scheme, but the generated schemes do not inherit an explicitly configured `DataProtectionProvider` from that source. Their tickets are protected with the application's default data protection provider instead of the provider configured for the source scheme.

Related to #66478 (DBSC tracking), #68117 (API proposal), and #69618 (derived session cookie path inheritance). The implementation was removed from .NET 11 by #69462 and backported by #69479, so this issue tracks a requirement for any future DBSC reintroduction rather than a .NET 11 servicing change.

## What is wrong

* Generated refresh and session schemes should use the same data protection configuration as their source scheme unless the application explicitly configures them differently.
* `PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.CopyFromSource` copies cookie attributes and lifetime settings but not `DataProtectionProvider`.
* Copying the provider only in the existing post-configure step would still be too late. `AddCookie` registers `PostConfigureCookieAuthenticationOptions` first; that component assigns the default provider and builds the fallback `TicketDataFormat` before DBSC's post-configure runs.
* The `AddDeviceBoundSession` surface does not document that generated schemes otherwise fall back to the default provider.

## Why it matters

* Applications that configure a dedicated provider on the source scheme, such as a dedicated key ring, application name, or key protection, expect credentials derived from that scheme to use the same protection configuration.
* In deployments where only the source scheme's provider is persisted or shared across instances, derived DBSC cookies can fail to unprotect after restart or on another instance even though source cookies work.

## Affected code

Permalinks point to `b3d5795c6f`, the last `main` commit before the DBSC removal.

* [`PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.cs:80-92`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.cs#L80-L92) - `CopyFromSource` omits `DataProtectionProvider`.
* [`PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.cs:30-56`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.cs#L30-L56) - generated-scheme post-configuration entry point.
* [`DeviceBoundSessionExtensions.cs:84-96`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/DeviceBoundSessionExtensions.cs#L84-L96) - generated refresh and session schemes registered through `AddCookie`.
* [`DeviceBoundSessionExtensions.cs:120-122`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/DeviceBoundSessionExtensions.cs#L120-L122) - DBSC options components registered only as `IPostConfigureOptions`.
* [`PostConfigureCookieAuthenticationOptions.cs:30-45`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/Cookies/src/PostConfigureCookieAuthenticationOptions.cs#L30-L45) - core cookie post-configure assigns the default provider and builds `TicketDataFormat`.
* [`CookieExtensions.cs:79`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/Cookies/src/CookieExtensions.cs#L79) - registration that places the core cookie post-configure ahead of DBSC's.
* [`DeviceBoundSessionCookieProtectionTests.cs:57-88`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/test/DeviceBoundSessions/DeviceBoundSessionCookieProtectionTests.cs#L57-L88) - existing coverage for per-scheme protection keying, but not provider inheritance.
* `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.DeviceBoundSessions` `0.11.0-rc.1.26425.128` - experimental prerelease package containing the implementation.

## Recommended fix

Assign the source provider during named configuration, before `PostConfigureCookieAuthenticationOptions` builds the fallback ticket format. Preserve an explicit derived-scheme provider or ticket format, and leave ticket-format construction to the core cookie post-configure so each generated scheme keeps its scheme-specific protector purpose.

```csharp
private void InheritDataProtection(string sourceScheme, CookieAuthenticationOptions target)
{
    if (target.DataProtectionProvider is not null ||
        target.TicketDataFormat is not null)
    {
        return;
    }

    var source = _services.GetRequiredService<IOptionsMonitor<CookieAuthenticationOptions>>().Get(sourceScheme);
    target.DataProtectionProvider = source.DataProtectionProvider;
}
```

* Have the derived-options component also implement `IConfigureNamedOptions<CookieAuthenticationOptions>`, apply the helper only to generated refresh and session scheme names, and register it for both named configuration and post-configuration in `AddDeviceBoundSessionCore`.
* Keep application configuration authoritative: an explicit provider or ticket format on a generated scheme is left unchanged.
* Document inheritance and override semantics on `AddDeviceBoundSession`.

Alternatives considered:

* Copy the provider in the existing post-configure step only. Rejected because the fallback `TicketDataFormat` already exists by then.
* Reuse the source scheme's `TicketDataFormat` instance. Rejected because it removes the per-scheme purpose separation between source, refresh, and session tickets.
* Require applications to configure each generated scheme. Rejected because generated scheme names are an implementation detail and the current surface does not disclose that requirement.
* Open question: define the expected derived-scheme behavior when the source uses a custom `TicketDataFormat` without a provider, or a `SessionStore` (see #67794).

Compatibility: no public API change is expected. After the change, derived cookies previously protected with a different provider will no longer unprotect, and affected browsers must re-register or re-authenticate. Because the package is experimental and removed from .NET 11, apply this before any future DBSC package is published.

## Acceptance criteria

* [ ] When the source scheme has an explicit `DataProtectionProvider`, tickets issued by the generated refresh and session schemes are protected with that provider rather than the application-default provider.
* [ ] An explicitly configured `DataProtectionProvider` or `TicketDataFormat` on a generated scheme is preserved.
* [ ] Source, refresh, and session tickets remain non-interchangeable; `DerivedCookieSchemes_RemainDataProtected_AndSchemeKeyed` continues to pass.
* [ ] Behavior without an explicit source provider is unchanged.
* [ ] Tests exercise the real `AddCookie` and `AddDeviceBoundSession` registration path, not only direct `PostConfigure` calls, so options-pipeline ordering is covered.
* [ ] `AddDeviceBoundSession` documentation describes provider inheritance and override semantics.
* [ ] #66478 records this requirement before DBSC is reintroduced.

Issues.Title: DBSC derived session cookie should preserve source cookie path
Issues.Body:
## Summary

The experimental DBSC implementation derived its session-cookie settings from a source cookie scheme but did not preserve an explicitly configured source cookie path. The derived session cookie must remain within the same path scope as the source credential.

Related to #66478 and the API proposal in #68117. The implementation was removed from .NET 11 by #69462 and backported by #69479, so this issue tracks a requirement for any future DBSC reintroduction rather than a .NET 11 servicing change.

## What is wrong

* `PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.CopyFromSource` copied `HttpOnly`, `SecurePolicy`, `SameSite`, `Domain`, and lifetime settings, but omitted `Cookie.Path`.
* The session-derived scheme therefore used its own default path instead of preserving an explicit path configured on the source cookie scheme.
* The refresh-derived scheme has separate intentional path behavior and should remain scoped to the configured DBSC refresh endpoint.

## Why it matters (defense in depth)

* Cookie derivation should not broaden the source cookie's configured scope as an unintended side effect.
* Preserving the source path maintains application-boundary isolation for deployments that host multiple applications under one origin.

## Affected code

* [`PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.cs:80-92`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/DeviceBoundSessions/src/PostConfigureDeviceBoundSessionDerivedCookieOptions.cs#L80-L92) (last `main` commit before removal) - `CopyFromSource` copied source-cookie attributes without copying `Cookie.Path`.
* [`DeviceBoundSessionCookieProtectionTests.cs:130-160`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b3d5795c6f8ffe4c25f0271ddcf66560f52ac377/src/Security/Authentication/test/DeviceBoundSessions/DeviceBoundSessionCookieProtectionTests.cs#L130-L160) (last `main` commit before removal) - covered inherited attributes but did not assert path inheritance.
* `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.DeviceBoundSessions` `0.11.0-rc.1.26425.128` - experimental prerelease package containing the implementation. The package was subsequently removed from .NET 11 by #69462 and #69479.

## Recommended fix

When DBSC is reintroduced, copy `source.Cookie.Path` to the derived session cookie alongside the other inherited cookie attributes. Keep the refresh cookie's explicitly computed DBSC endpoint path unchanged. Add focused tests with a non-root source-cookie path that assert the session cookie builds with the same path and the refresh cookie continues to use its dedicated endpoint scope.

Copying the complete `CookieBuilder` was considered but is not preferred because the derived schemes intentionally differ in name, lifetime behavior, and refresh-path handling. Changing the global cookie defaults was also rejected because the invariant belongs specifically to derivation from the configured source scheme.

This is an internal options-wiring correction with no expected public API change or migration requirement. Because the implementation is no longer present in .NET 11, the correction should be included in the branch where DBSC development resumes and covered before another package is published.

## Acceptance criteria

* [ ] A derived DBSC session cookie preserves an explicitly configured `Cookie.Path` from its source cookie scheme.
* [ ] A derived DBSC refresh cookie remains scoped to the configured refresh endpoint rather than inheriting the source path.
* [ ] Regression tests cover a non-root source path and assert both derived-cookie behaviors.
* [ ] Default-path and request-path-base behavior remain unchanged when the source does not explicitly configure `Cookie.Path`.

Issues.Title: WsFederationHandler discards AuthenticationProperties replaced in OnSecurityTokenReceived
Issues.Body:
## Summary

`WsFederationHandler.HandleRemoteAuthenticateAsync` ignores an `AuthenticationProperties` instance assigned to `SecurityTokenReceivedContext.Properties` by an `OnSecurityTokenReceived` handler. After the event returns, the handler reads properties back from the earlier `MessageReceivedContext`, so a wholesale replacement never reaches `SecurityTokenValidated` or the issued `AuthenticationTicket`.

## What is wrong

* Remote authentication events expose `Properties` as a settable property (`RemoteAuthenticationContext.Properties { get; set; }`). The handler contract, as implemented by `OpenIdConnectHandler`, is that after each event the handler flows `properties` from **that event's own context**.
* `WsFederationHandler` breaks this after `SecurityTokenReceived`: it runs `properties = messageReceivedContext.Properties!;` instead of reading `securityTokenReceivedContext.Properties`.
* In-place mutation (`context.Properties.Items[...] = ...`) still works because by default all contexts share one instance. Only reference replacement (`context.Properties = new AuthenticationProperties(...)`) is lost.
* The line appears to be a copy/paste slip carried over from the original port. It has been unchanged since at least the file-scoped namespace conversion (a450cb69b5, #38076).

## Why it matters (defense in depth)

* Correctness: a documented, public, settable event property is silently ignored. Application code that replaces properties in `OnSecurityTokenReceived` (for example, to set `RedirectUri`, `IsPersistent`, `ExpiresUtc`, or custom `Items`) gets the pre-event values in `OnSecurityTokenValidated`, `OnTicketReceived`, and the sign-in cookie, with no error.
* Consistency: every other flow point in `WsFederationHandler` (`MessageReceived`, `SecurityTokenValidated`) and all equivalent points in `OpenIdConnectHandler` honor replacement. Aligning WS-Federation removes a surprising divergence between the two federation handlers.
* Hardening: app-supplied authentication state set in an event must reach the ticket as written. Anti-forgery correlation validation happens before this event and does not depend on this code path, and token validation does not consume these properties. The fix makes event-to-ticket state flow predictable. It does not change any framework validation decision.

## Affected code

Paths are relative to the repo root, at `main` 8821f7eb71.

* `src/Security/Authentication/WsFederation/src/WsFederationHandler.cs:233-243` - `SecurityTokenReceivedContext` is created and raised, then line 243 reads properties from `messageReceivedContext` (defect).
* `src/Security/Authentication/WsFederation/src/WsFederationHandler.cs:211` - correct pattern for `MessageReceived` (reads its own context).
* `src/Security/Authentication/WsFederation/src/WsFederationHandler.cs:316-347` - downstream consumers: `UseTokenLifetime` writes to `properties`, `SecurityTokenValidatedContext` is built from it, and line 347 flows the result into the ticket.
* `src/Security/Authentication/Core/src/Events/RemoteAuthenticationContext.cs:25-37` - `Properties` is `public virtual { get; set; }`. The constructor substitutes a new instance when passed null.
* `src/Security/Authentication/OpenIdConnect/src/OpenIdConnectHandler.cs:700,799,824,844,884,1094` - reference pattern: each event's own context is read back.
* Tests: `src/Security/Authentication/test/WsFederation/WsFederationTest.cs` (`ValidTokenIsAccepted` at 124-146, `CreateClient` at 281, unawaited `AuthenticateAsync` in terminal endpoint at 428) and `WsFederationTest_Handler.cs` (`ValidTokenIsAccepted` at 115-137, `CreateClient` at 272, terminal endpoint at 417). The two files cover the `UseSecurityTokenHandlers = true` and `TokenHandlers` validation paths and should both get the regression test.

A sweep of the other remote handlers in `src/Security/Authentication` (OAuth, Twitter, OpenIdConnect, Negotiate, Certificate, JwtBearer, Cookies) found no other instance of this pattern.

## Recommended fix

**Selected approach.** Replace line 243 with:

```csharp
properties = securityTokenReceivedContext.Properties ?? properties;
```

This flows a replacement instance forward. The `?? properties` fallback keeps today's behavior if a handler explicitly assigns `null`: processing continues with the pre-event instance instead of hitting a `NullReferenceException` in the `UseTokenLifetime` block or `SecurityTokenValidatedContext`. No other lines change. Result short-circuiting, correlation validation, token validation, lifetime handling, and the `SecurityTokenValidated` flow stay as they are.

**Alternatives considered.**

* `properties = securityTokenReceivedContext.Properties!;` (exact OIDC style). Rejected: explicit `null` would now fail authentication through `AuthenticationFailed` instead of proceeding. That is a behavior change with no benefit.
* Leave the code and document "mutate, don't replace". Rejected: it contradicts the public settable property and the behavior of every other event.
* Refactor the method to carry properties only through contexts. Rejected: unnecessary churn for a one-line defect.

**Compatibility.**

* No public API change. No `PublicAPI.*.txt` updates.
* Behavior change only for apps that assign a new instance to `SecurityTokenReceivedContext.Properties`. Those apps get the documented behavior they asked for. Apps that mutate in place or don't handle the event are unaffected because the reference is unchanged.
* A replacement instance drops `.xsrf`, `RedirectUri`, and the user-state item unless the app copies them. This is already true for replacement in `MessageReceived`/`SecurityTokenValidated`. Correlation is validated before this event, so dropping `.xsrf` there has no effect. A missing `RedirectUri` falls back to `/` in `RemoteAuthenticationHandler`.
* Suitable for `main`. Servicing is optional and low risk given the one-line scope.

## Acceptance criteria

* [ ] After `OnSecurityTokenReceived` assigns a new `AuthenticationProperties` instance, `SecurityTokenValidatedContext.Properties` is that same instance (reference equality).
* [ ] Custom `Items` from the replacement instance persist into the issued ticket (observable through `AuthenticateAsync()` on the cookie scheme in a follow-up request).
* [ ] In-place mutation of `SecurityTokenReceivedContext.Properties.Items` still flows to the ticket (existing behavior preserved).
* [ ] Assigning `null` in `OnSecurityTokenReceived` still completes sign-in with the pre-event properties (no new failure mode).
* [ ] Regression tests are added to both `WsFederationTest.cs` and `WsFederationTest_Handler.cs`. Each test fails on current `main` (replacement not observed) and passes with the fix. Suggested harness change: add an optional `Action<WsFederationEvents>? configureEvents` parameter to each `CreateClient` helper that wraps existing handlers, and `await` the currently unawaited `context.AuthenticateAsync()` in the terminal endpoint so a test can read `result.Properties`.
* [ ] `./src/Security/build.sh -test` (or `build.cmd -test`) passes for the WsFederation test classes.

Issues.Title: Response compression: add a minimum response size threshold (MinimumSize)
Issues.Body:
Related to #5994. I'd like to work on this, but wanted to check the design with you first.

Right now there's no way to skip compression for small responses, even though the response compression docs say not to compress anything under roughly 150-1000 bytes. Express's compression middleware has a `threshold` option (1kb by default), nginx has `gzip_min_length`, and Spring Boot has `server.compression.min-response-size` (2048 bytes by default). Express is the closest match since it's also a middleware.

My idea is an `int MinimumSize` on `ResponseCompressionOptions`, defaulting to 0 so existing apps behave the same. If Content-Length is known and smaller than that, the response isn't compressed and no Content-Encoding header is added. If there's no Content-Length it's compressed like today, so nothing gets buffered, which is how Tratcher and davidfowl described it in #5994. I'd update PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt and add tests for below, at and above the threshold, plus a streaming case.

There's also #58737, which proposes disabling compression per endpoint and lists a `Predict`-style callback as an alternative design. A callback could cover the size case too by checking Content-Length, but a plain `MinimumSize` is simpler to configure and is what Express, nginx and Spring Boot offer. Would you rather have the threshold on its own, or should this go through the callback approach from #58737?

Issues.Title: Negotiate: bound nested-group recursion depth in LdapAdapter.GetNestedGroups
Issues.Body:
## Summary

`LdapAdapter.GetNestedGroups` resolves nested group membership recursively without any upper bound on the recursion depth. Call-stack consumption therefore depends entirely on the shape of the data returned by the configured directory.

## What is wrong

* Nested-group traversal is unbounded: the depth of the managed call stack equals the length of the longest `memberOf` chain returned by the directory.
* The existing `processedGroups` set (added in #38817) prevents revisiting a group, which handles circular references, but it does not limit the depth of an acyclic chain of distinct groups.
* A stack overflow in .NET cannot be caught and terminates the whole process, so a failure here affects every request served by the host, not only the current authentication.
* The traversal runs before the result is stored in the claims cache, so the same directory data would hit the same behavior again after a restart.

## Why it matters (defense in depth)

* Correctness: library code that consumes external data should not allow that data to decide how much stack is used. Real-world directories with very deep group nesting are already considered a misconfiguration, and a bounded traversal fails gracefully instead of crashing the host.
* Hardening: the configured directory is a trusted claims authority, but the authentication handler should remain resilient if that authority is misconfigured, contains unusually deep hierarchies, or returns unexpected data. A depth limit turns an uncatchable process failure into a bounded, loggable condition.

## Affected code

* `src/Security/Authentication/Negotiate/src/Internal/LdapAdapter.cs:98` - entry point that starts the nested traversal for each direct `memberOf` group
* `src/Security/Authentication/Negotiate/src/Internal/LdapAdapter.cs:126-172` - `GetNestedGroups` recursion, visited-set tracking, and recursive call
* `src/Security/Authentication/Negotiate/src/LdapSettings.cs` - `IgnoreNestedGroups` is the only existing control over nested resolution

## Recommended fix

**Selected approach:** add a maximum nesting depth to `GetNestedGroups`. Pass the current depth as a parameter, increment it on each recursive call, and stop traversing (returning without recursing further) once the limit is reached. A single fixed limit also bounds any acyclic chain and any cycle that might slip past the visited set, so depth becomes the one invariant guaranteeing termination and bounded stack use.

Design decisions:

* Use an internal constant (for example, 32 or 64 levels; legitimate directory nesting is far shallower) so no public API is introduced. Choose a value comfortably below the stack budget of a default thread.
* When the limit is reached, stop descending, keep the claims already collected, and emit a single `LogWarning` (or a source-generated log message following the existing logging conventions in this project) identifying that nested group resolution was truncated. Do not log group names from the directory beyond what existing messages already log.
* Keep the visited-set check so repeated groups are still skipped cheaply and cycles do not consume the full depth budget.
* Review the existing `return` inside the `foreach` over `memberof` when a visited group is found: it currently abandons the remaining sibling groups. Decide deliberately whether to change it to `continue` as part of this work, or leave it for a separate change, since it affects which claims are returned.

**Alternatives considered:**

* Convert the recursion to an iterative traversal with an explicit work queue. This removes stack dependence entirely, but it is a larger change to a security-sensitive path and still benefits from a total-work cap; it can be a follow-up.
* Add a public `LdapSettings` option for the maximum depth. This adds public API surface that would need API review; an internal constant is sufficient for the hardening goal, and a setting can be added later if a real need appears.
* Use `RuntimeHelpers.EnsureSufficientExecutionStack()`. This throws a catchable exception before overflow, but the limit depends on the remaining stack at that moment and produces less predictable behavior than a fixed depth.

**Compatibility and behavior:**

* Existing deployments with realistic group nesting are unaffected as long as the limit is well above typical depth.
* Deployments with nesting beyond the limit will receive claims for groups up to the limit only. This should be documented in the XML docs for `LdapSettings.IgnoreNestedGroups` or the relevant docs page, and in the log message.
* No public API changes are required, so no API review is needed.

## Acceptance criteria

* [ ] `GetNestedGroups` never recurses deeper than the defined maximum, regardless of the directory data.
* [ ] A chain of distinct groups longer than the maximum completes without crashing and returns claims only up to the limit.
* [ ] Circular references still terminate correctly, and existing circular-reference behavior is preserved.
* [ ] Reaching the limit is logged once per resolution rather than once per group.
* [ ] Unit tests in `src/Security/Authentication/Negotiate/test/Negotiate.Test` cover below-limit, exactly-at-limit, above-limit, and circular hierarchies, using a mocked or fake `LdapConnection` response source (the current `LdapAdapter` tests do not yet exercise the nested-group path, so a seam for the connection may be needed).
* [ ] Behavior when the limit is reached is documented.

## Summary

Issues.Title: Cookie name matching is case-insensitive, diverging from RFC 6265's case-sensitive semantics
Issues.Body:
RFC 6265 (§4.1.1, §5.3) specifies that cookie names are matched case-sensitively when a browser stores, updates, or looks up a cookie. ASP.NET Core, however, treats cookie names case-insensitively throughout its cookie-handling APIs. `RequestCookieCollection` parses the incoming `Cookie` header into a dictionary using [`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/92b29c372eb45d57c415b01b06b41a3a8c439ed6/src/Http/Http/src/Internal/RequestCookieCollection.cs#L30), so   `Request.Cookies["MyCookie"]` and `Request.Cookies["mycookie"]` resolve to the same entry even though a client can legitimately hold two distinct, separately-stored cookies differing only by case.

We need to match RFC and treat cookie case sensitively. We would need to announce a breaking change for consumers about this change.

Issues.Title: .NET 10 OpenAPI emits an object constraint for floating-point values
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues.

### Describe the bug

With `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` **10.0.12**, enabling `JsonNumberHandling.AllowNamedFloatingPointLiterals` generates an unsatisfiable schema for a `double` property. The endpoint returns numeric values, but its OpenAPI 3.1.1 schema requires an object alongside number/string alternatives:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "anyOf": [
    {
      "pattern": "^-?(?:0|[1-9]\\d*)(?:\\.\\d+)?(?:[eE][+-]?\\d+)?$",
      "type": ["number", "string"]
    },
    {
      "enum": ["NaN", "Infinity", "-Infinity"]
    }
  ],
  "format": "double"
}
```

A number fails the object constraint; an object fails both alternatives. No JSON value satisfies this schema.

### Expected Behavior

Keep the numeric and named-literal alternatives without the outer `"type": "object"` constraint.

### Steps To Reproduce

[Reproduction repository](https://github.com/alexaka1/repro-dotnet--aspnetcore-openapi-floating-point)

```sh
git clone https://github.com/alexaka1/repro-dotnet--aspnetcore-openapi-floating-point.git
cd repro-dotnet--aspnetcore-openapi-floating-point
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose run --rm compare
```

The repro changes two things in `dotnet new webapi`: enables `AllowNamedFloatingPointLiterals` through `ConfigureHttpJsonOptions` and changes `WeatherForecast.TemperatureF` from `int` to `double`.

The comparison runs the same source on both versions and prints the response value and `temperatureF` schema.

### Exceptions (if any)

None. Both endpoints return HTTP 200.

### .NET Version

SDK **10.0.401**, ASP.NET Core and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` **10.0.12**.

### Anything else?

| Runtime and OpenAPI package | Native ARM64 | Emulated x64 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10.0.12 | Incorrect object constraint | Incorrect object constraint |
| 11.0.0-preview.6.26359.118 | Correct numeric alternatives | Correct numeric alternatives |

The bug is architecture-independent. Each version produced identical documents on native ARM64 and x64 under Docker emulation on an ARM64 host. The .NET 10 containers ran Ubuntu 24.04 and reported `linux-arm64` and `linux-x64`, respectively.

[`OpenApiJsonSchema.ReadProperty`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/v10.0.12/src/OpenApi/src/Schemas/OpenApiJsonSchema.Helpers.cs#L298-L308) unconditionally sets `schema.Type = JsonSchemaType.Object` when reading `anyOf` or `oneOf`. #67001 removes that assignment as part of union support. The comparison above verifies the corrected behavior in .NET 11 Preview 6.

Could this correction be considered for a .NET 10 servicing release?

Issues.Title: Add agent guidance for AzDO and Helix CI investigation
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Add repository-specific Copilot guidance for diagnosing and retrying Azure Pipelines and Helix failures on ASP.NET Core pull requests.

## Motivation and goals

Agent-driven CI investigations currently require rediscovering several ASP.NET Core-specific distinctions that materially affect the correct response to a red aggregate:

- A failed Azure Pipelines aggregate may represent a product/test failure, pre-Helix restore failure, Helix submission failure, post-test reporter failure, merge conflict, or unrelated infrastructure problem.
- GitHub's check-run rerequest endpoint may not support Azure Pipelines external checks.
- A retry should be scoped to the affected pipeline and should occur only after every failure is attributed.

For example, #69232 had two failed `signalr.client.java.Tests--` Helix work items even though every Java test passed. Both failed later in Gradle `:test:testReport` because Spotless could not load JGit `AnyObjectId`. The MVC-only diff had no correlation, and a target-branch build using the same target SHA passed both Windows Helix subsets. A scoped `/azp run aspnetcore-ci` queued a replacement build, which passed along with Build Analysis and Build Insights.

Other recent investigations have encountered materially different red states, including restore failures before any Helix work item was submitted, Helix submission HTTP failures, and merge conflicts where no AzDO build was queued. Durable guidance would make classifications and retry decisions more consistent and evidence-based.

## In scope

- Add a dedicated `.github/instructions/ci.instructions.md` or an equivalent focused section in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`.
- Require resolving every red aggregate to its exact AzDO build and job and, when present, its Helix work item and failure stage.
- Require correlation with changed files, Build Analysis/known-issue evidence, target-branch comparison, and build progression as applicable.
- Explicitly distinguish product/test failures from restore, submission, reporter, post-test, merge-conflict, and infrastructure failures.
- Document the scoped `/azp run <pipeline-name>` retry path for Azure Pipelines checks when GitHub rerequest is unsupported.
- Require verifying bot acknowledgement, replacement build ID, PR source SHA, and final Build Analysis/Build Insights state.
- Prohibit empty commits as a CI retry mechanism.

## Out of scope

- Changing Azure Pipelines or Helix infrastructure.
- Automatically classifying failures without log evidence.
- Creating or expanding Known Build Error issues.
- Repository-specific guidance for non-AzDO CI systems.

## Risks / unknowns

- Guidance could duplicate or drift from Arcade's Build Analysis documentation; the repository instruction should link to or align with the authoritative workflow rather than restating unstable implementation details.
- Pipeline names and retry-comment behavior may evolve, so examples should emphasize the decision process and scoped retry principle.
- The instruction's `applyTo` scope needs to cover PR/CI maintenance tasks without affecting unrelated code-authoring prompts.

## Examples

Suggested core guidance:

> Do not classify or retry a red Azure Pipelines aggregate until every failure is resolved to its exact build, job, and—when present—Helix work item and failure stage. Correlate the signature with changed files and build progression, compare the target branch and known-issue evidence where needed, and distinguish product/test failures from restore, submission, reporter, post-test, merge-conflict, and infrastructure failures. Retry only after attribution; for external AzDO checks use the repository's scoped `/azp run <pipeline-name>` path when GitHub rerequest is unsupported, and verify the replacement build was actually queued. Never use an empty commit as a retry mechanism.

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)

Issues.Title: Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019
Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "[Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time" (#537)

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

Issues.Title: Add automation to create docs tracking issues for breaking changes
Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

## Security

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**
```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**
```csharp
using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

Both Copilot and ChatGpt have given good results so far when asked to convert a WebHostBuilder example to use HostBuilder. Below is an example prompt:
<details>
<summary>Example AI Prompt</summary>

> Can you convert
>
> var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

### Affected APIs

`public class Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.WebHostBuilder`
`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`

### Discussion

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/63480

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and MVC API analyzers are deprecated
Issues.Body:
## Description

The `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` MSBuild property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. When `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will now emit warning `ASPDEPR007`.

## Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

## Previous behavior

Previously, developers could set `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` in their Web SDK projects to enable MVC API analyzers without any warnings or deprecation notices.

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

The project would build successfully without any deprecation warnings.

## New behavior

Starting in .NET 10 Preview 7, when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will emit warning `ASPDEPR007`:

```
warning ASPDEPR007: The IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
```

The analyzers will continue to function, but developers will receive this deprecation warning during compilation.

## Type of breaking change

- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

## Reason for change

## Reason for change

The MVC API analyzers were originally introduced to help keep return types and attributes in sync for API controllers, ensuring consistency between method signatures and their corresponding OpenAPI documentation. These analyzers provided compile-time validation to catch mismatches between declared return types and the actual types returned by controller actions.

However, with the introduction of Minimal APIs and the `TypedResults` pattern, the .NET ecosystem has evolved toward a more type-safe approach for API development. `TypedResults` provides compile-time guarantees about response types without requiring additional analyzers, making the MVC API analyzers redundant for modern .NET applications. In .NET 10, `TypedResults` are supported in controller-based APIs.

**Previous approach with MVC API analyzers:**
```csharp
[HttpGet]
[ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)]
[ProducesResponseType(404)]
public async Task<ActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    if (product == null)
        return NotFound(); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType(404)
    
    return Ok(product); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)
}
```

**Or with controller actions using TypedResults:**
```csharp
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    return product == null 
        ? TypedResults.NotFound() 
        : TypedResults.Ok(product);
}
```

The `TypedResults` pattern eliminates the need for separate analyzers because the return type itself (`Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>`) explicitly declares all possible response types at compile time. This approach is more maintainable, provides better IntelliSense support, and automatically generates accurate OpenAPI documentation without additional tooling.

As the .NET ecosystem continues to embrace `TypedResults` as the recommended pattern for API development, the MVC API analyzers have become obsolete and are being deprecated to streamline the development experience.

## Recommended action

Developers should:

1. **Remove the deprecated property**: Remove `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` from your project files to eliminate the warning.

2. **Suppress the warning temporarily**: If you need to continue using the deprecated analyzers temporarily, you can suppress the warning:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ASPDEPR007</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

3. **Migrate to TypedResults**: Migrate to the `TypedResults` pattern documented above to ensure better consistency between application behavior and OpenAPI documentation.

## Affected APIs

- MSBuild property: `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers`
- Associated MVC API analyzers included when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is `true`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Forwarded Headers Middleware Now Ignores X-Forwarded-* Headers from Unknown Proxies
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 8.0.17 and 9.0.6, the Forwarded Headers Middleware will ignore all `X-Forwarded-*` headers from proxies that are not explicitly configured as trusted.

### Version

.NET 8

### Previous behavior

Previously, the middleware, when not configured to use `X-Forwarded-For`, would process `X-Forwarded-Prefix`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and `X-Forwarded-Host` headers from any source, potentially allowing malicious or misconfigured proxies/clients to spoof these headers and affect your application's understanding of client information.

### New behavior

With this change, only headers sent by known, trusted proxies (as configured via `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownProxies` and `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownNetworks`) will be processed. Headers from unknown sources will be ignored.

**This is a breaking change**: If your deployment relied on forwarded headers from proxies not configured in your application's trusted proxy list, those headers will no longer be honored.

This can cause behavior like infinite redirects if you're using the Https redirection middleware and using TLS termination in your proxy. Or authentication to fail if using TLS termination and expecting an https request.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The change was made for security hardening, as the proxy and IP lists weren't being applied in all cases.

### Recommended action

- **Review your deployment topology:**  
  Ensure that all legitimate proxy servers in front of your app are properly added to `KnownProxies` or `KnownNetworks` in your `ForwardedHeadersOptions` configuration.
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownProxies = { IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_PROXY_IP") }
  });
  ```
  Or, for a network:
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownNetworks = { new IPNetwork(IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_NETWORK_IP"), PREFIX_LENGTH) }
  });
  ```

- **If you wish to enable previous behavior:**  
  You may need to relax your configuration, but this is **not recommended** due to security risks. You can do this by clearing the `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies` lists in `ForwardedHeadersOptions` to allow any proxy or network to forward these headers.

You can also set the `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` environment variable to true, which clears the lists and enables `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto`.

For applications targeting .NET 9.0 or less, you can set the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpOverrides.IgnoreUnknownProxiesWithoutFor` [AppContext](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/runtime-libraries/system-appcontext) switch to `"true"` or `1` to get back to the previous behavior. Alternatively, set the `MICROSOFT_ASPNETCORE_HTTPOVERRIDES_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_PROXIES_WITHOUT_FOR` environment variable.

> [!Note]
> In cloud environments, the proxy IP(s) can change over the lifetime of the app and `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` is sometimes used to make forwarded headers work.

### References

- [Forwarded Headers Middleware documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/host-and-deploy/proxy-load-balancer)

### Affected APIs

`UseForwardedHeaders();`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: dev cert export no longer creates folder
Issues.Body:
### Description

When you export the ASP.NET Core development certificate (used to enable https in local development), it will no longer create the directory into which the certificate is being exported, if that directory doesn’t already exist.

This change first appears in 8.0.10 and 9.0 RC1.

### Version

.NET 8 GA

### Previous behavior

```
dotnet dev-certs https -ep C:\NonExistent\cert.pfx
```

If `C:\NonExistent\` did not exist when the command was run, it would be created (with permissions inherited from the containing directory).

### New behavior

The target directory must exist or the export will fail with a message like `There was an error exporting the HTTPS developer certificate to a file.`

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The development certificate is exported with its private key, so unauthorized access can be very problematic.  It may, nevertheless, be necessary to make it readable to multiple accounts - e.g. if the consuming process will not be run as the current user.  Rather than attempting to determine (and securely establish) permissions for the target directory, `dotnet dev-certs` require that it already exist.

### Recommended action

Create the target directory (with appropriate permissions) before invoking `dotnet dev-certs`.

### Affected APIs

This functionality is not presently exposed via an API - it is invoked from the command line.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Handling of middleware types with multiple constructors
Issues.Body:
### Description

Formerly, when a middleware type with multiple satisfiable constructors was instantiated from the dependency injection container, the one with the most parameters would be used.  Now that only happens if the dependency injection container implements [`IServiceProviderIsService`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.iserviceproviderisservice).

### Version

.NET 9 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Formerly, the first constructor was preferred (when both were satisfied) because it has more parameters.

```csharp
public class CookiePolicyMiddleware
{
    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options, ILoggerFactory factory)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }

    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }
}
```

### New behavior

Now, neither constructor is preferred and construction fails with an error like 
```
System.InvalidOperationException: 'Multiple constructors accepting all given argument types have been found in type 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware'. There should only be one applicable constructor.'
```

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The activation mechanism was [changed](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/55722) to help support keyed dependency injection.

### Recommended action

If this happens and you can't upgrade to a dependency injection container that implements `IServiceProviderIsService`, you can add `ActivatorUtilitiesConstructorAttribute` to the preferred constructor of the affected middleware type.

### Affected APIs

This is [known](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/57231) to cause errors when instantiating `Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware` with [Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection) 7.x.
